The Permission to Notice

There is a particular kind of quiet that exists only on a weekday afternoon in a small city, when most people are indoors doing whatever it is that people do, and the streets belong to the old, the very young, and the unemployable. I found myself in that quiet once, not by choice but by circumstance, sitting on a bench outside a post office with nothing to do and nowhere to be. I had no phone. I had no book. I had only the afternoon, and the strange, uncomfortable gift of being unoccupied.

At first it felt like a kind of poverty. I watched a pigeon walk a circle around a discarded sandwich wrapper, its head bobbing with that mechanical certainty pigeons have, as if they are always nodding at an invisible metronome. I watched a woman emerge from the post office with a cardboard tube under her arm, glance at the sky, and then walk left, out of my life forever. I watched a cloud move across the sun and change the temperature of my own skin by a degree. None of this mattered. None of this would make a difference in any ledger of achievement. And yet, sitting there, I began to feel something I had almost forgotten: the texture of being present.

We live in an age of constant interruption, but more than that, we live in an age of constant invitation. Every device in our pocket is a door to somewhere else, and we walk through those doors thousands of times a day, so often that we forget we are walking anywhere at all. We flit from one small screen to the next like a dragonfly skimming a pond, touching the surface of a thousand things but never sinking into any of them. The result is a peculiar kind of exhaustion, not from doing too much, but from being nowhere fully. We are always almost somewhere else. The present moment becomes a waiting room, and the only escape is the next notification, the next scroll, the next small hit of novelty.

I have been thinking about attention lately, not as a skill or a productivity hack, but as a form of love. To pay attention to something is to say, with your whole body, that it matters. When you really look at a leaf, you are not merely registering its shape and color; you are entering into a relationship with it. You are giving it your time, and time is the only currency we truly have. The leaf, of course, does not know or care. But you are changed by the looking. The act of attention is a kind of hospitality, an offering of the self to the world, and in that offering, you receive the world back, not as a series of data points, but as a presence.

I used to walk the same route to work every day, and I could not have told you a single thing about it. The route took me past a bakery, a park, a row of brownstones, and a construction site. I was in my head, rehearsing conversations, composing emails, worrying about the future, rewriting the past. The physical world was a blur at the edge of a mental movie. Then one day, a friend told me about a practice she called “the first ten minutes,” in which she forced herself, every morning, to walk the route without any internal narration. No planning, no judging, no commentary. Just the sensation of walking. The first time she tried it, she said, she noticed that the bakery had a green awning, and that it had been there for years, and that she had never seen it. She noticed that the park had a particular smell, like damp earth and cut grass, and that the brownstones each had a different kind of door handle, some brass, some iron, some glass. She noticed that the construction site had a mural painted on its plywood fence, and the mural had a small, painted bird in the corner, and the bird looked like it was winking.

I tried her practice the next morning, and it was agonizing. My mind rebelled. It wanted to think. It wanted to plan. It wanted to be anywhere but here, in the ordinary world. But I kept at it, and after a week, something shifted. The world began to appear. Not all at once, but in fragments, like a photograph developing in a tray of chemicals. I noticed that the bakery had a green awning. I noticed the door handles. I noticed the bird. And I realized, with a kind of shock, that I had been walking through an extraordinary world and seeing almost none of it.

Attention is not just a matter of looking; it is a matter of being willing to be affected. There is a vulnerability in it. When you truly look at something, you cannot remain entirely separate from it. The boundary between self and world softens. The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that “attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” I think she meant that to give attention is to give your own inner life to something outside yourself, to suspend your own concerns long enough to let another thing be real. It is an act of self-emptying, and in a culture that tells us constantly to self-promote, to self-express, to self-optimize, self-emptying is almost countercultural.

I have found that attention can be trained, but not in the way we usually think of training. It is not about forcing yourself to concentrate harder, or enduring the boredom of a task until it becomes automatic. It is more like cultivating a habit of receptivity, a posture of openness. You cannot force yourself to notice things with the same determination you would use to lift a weight. You have to relax into noticing. You have to become, as the poet John Keats put it, a “negative capability,” a person capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason.

One of the best ways I know to do this is to walk without a destination. Not a power walk, not a hike with a goal at the end, but a ramble, a saunter, a stroll with no purpose other than to see. The word “saunter” is said to come from the Middle Ages, when pilgrims walked to the Holy Land, and people asked them where they were going. They would answer, “à la sainte terre,” to the holy land. Whether or not that etymology is true, I like to think of a walk as a pilgrimage to the only holy land that exists: the present moment. And when you walk that way, the world becomes a text, and you learn to read it.

I remember one autumn afternoon, during a period when I was deeply unhappy, I went for a walk in a neighborhood I had never visited. It was a residential area, unremarkable, with identical houses on identical streets. I was not expecting much. But as I walked, I began to notice that every house had a small detail that made it unique: a mailbox shaped like a barn, a wind chime made of seashells, a porch swing with a faded cushion, a garden gnome holding a tiny fishing rod. I became fascinated. I started to invent stories for each house. The barn mailbox belonged to a retired farmer who missed the Midwest. The seashell wind chime was hung by a woman who had never seen the ocean but dreamed of it. The porch swing was used every evening by a couple who had nothing to say to each other but liked sitting in silence together. The gnome with the fishing rod was a gift from a son who had died years ago, and now the gnome was all the family the old man had left. I knew, of course, that all these stories were false. But they were not meaningless. They were my way of paying attention, of giving each object the dignity of a story, of treating the world as if it were alive and full of meaning. And by the end of the walk, my unhappiness had not disappeared, but it had been put into perspective. I was not the only one with a story. Everyone and everything had one. I was part of a vast, interwoven narrative, and I had forgotten it.

There is a particular joy in noticing the small things that are easy to dismiss. I am thinking of the way light falls through a glass of water onto a white tablecloth, making a tiny, trembling rainbow. I am thinking of the sound of rain at different times of day, how it patters in the morning and drums at night. I am thinking of the way a spider web catches the dew, each droplet a tiny lens, the whole structure a piece of jewelry made by a blind artisan. To notice these things is to be rich in a way that cannot be taxed or taken away. They are not experiences you can have only once; they are recurring, endless, free. In a world that is always trying to sell you the next new thing, these small things are the oldest things, the eternal things, and they are waiting for you on every street corner, in every patch of grass, in every empty moment.

But attention is not always pleasant. To notice the world is also to notice its wounds. There is the plastic bag caught in the branches of a tree, which will be there for decades, a small monument to our carelessness. There is the crushed soda can on the sidewalk, the broken bottle, the graffiti that is not art but anger. There is the man sleeping on a bench in the park, and you notice that he has no socks, and you notice that it is October, and you notice that you have a home to go to and he does not. Attention is not a vacation. It is a willingness to be present to everything, the beautiful and the terrible. And if you are willing to be present to the terrible, you may be moved to act, to make a small difference, to offer a blanket or a dollar or just the recognition that he is a person, not a piece of the landscape.

I have come to believe that attention is also a form of resistance. The forces of distraction—the algorithms, the advertisers, the 24-hour news cycle—want you to be scattered, reactive, anxious, and numb. They want you to scroll past your own life. They want you to believe that the only meaningful moments are the ones you can photograph, share, and monetize. They want you to be always elsewher. To pay attention, relentlessly and joyfully, to the world in front of you is to refuse that bargain. It is to say: my life is here, not on your screen. It is to reclaim your own time, moment by moment, from the great, sucking vacuum of manufactured urgency. And it is to remember that the reality of the world is infinitely more complex, strange, and beautiful than anything the machine can feed you.

There is a practice in Zen Buddhism called “beginner’s mind.” It means approaching the world as if you are seeing it for the first time, without the filters of expectation or habit. I am not a Buddhist, but I have tried to cultivate this. I have tried to look at a coffee cup as if I had never seen one before: the smooth curve of the ceramic, the small chip on the rim, the way the steam rises in a spiral. I have tried to listen to a bird song without identifying the bird, hearing it purely as sound, a wild and intricate melody with no purpose but itself. I have tried to taste a piece of bread as if it were the first food I had ever eaten, noticing the sweetness of the crust, the soft crumb, the faint tang of salt. These experiments are hard. My mind wants to label, categorize, and move on. It wants to turn the coffee cup into the concept of a coffee cup and then stop seeing it. But when I can keep the beginner’s mind, even for a few minutes, the world becomes new again. I am no longer walking through a familiar landscape. I am walking through a miracle.

Time is strange when you pay attention. It does not pass in a uniform flow; it expands and contracts, deepens and thins. An hour spent scrolling through your phone can feel like five minutes, and afterward you cannot remember a single thing you saw. But five minutes spent watching a sunset can feel like an hour, and the memory of it can last a lifetime. Attention is the key to this mystery. When you are fully present, time slows down. It becomes thick, textured, rich. You are no longer a passive passenger, being carried toward the grave. You are an active participant, and every moment is a doorway into something larger than yourself. This is why children often seem to live in a different temporal world: they have not yet learned to rush. Everything is new to them, and so everything is worthy of attention. A puddle is a small ocean. A bug is a dragon. A cardboard box is a house. To recover this capacity is not to become childish, but to become wise.

I think of the writer and naturalist Henry David Thoreau, who built a cabin at Walden Pond and spent two years paying attention to the world around him. He wrote about the color of the ice, the flight of a hawk, the sound of a train in the distance. His book “Walden” is not really a book about nature; it is a book about attention. He went to the woods, he said, “to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach.” He did not need to travel to a distant country. The whole universe, he believed, was present in the rhythm of a single day, if you could only see it. For two years, an American writer paid attention, and out of that attention came a book that has touched millions of lives. The rest of us, perhaps, do not need to build a cabin. We need only to put down our phones and look out the window. We need only to take a walk without a destination. We need only to be willing to be bored, because in boredom the mind finally stops jumping and begins to settle, and when it settles, the world can appear.

But we are afraid of boredom. We have built an entire civilization to avoid it. We have invented endless forms of entertainment, distraction, and mere stimulation. We have made it possible to go from birth to death without ever being alone with our thoughts for a single moment. And yet boredom, paradoxically, is one of the most fertile states of mind. It is the fallow field. When we are bored, we are not doing anything, and in not doing anything, we open ourselves to the unexpected. The great aphorist and essayist Blaise Pascal wrote, “All of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.” He was not saying that we should never act. He was saying that we have lost the ability to be still, to be present, to pay attention, and from that stillness all true action should arise. The solution to our frenetic, anxious age is not more activity, more productivity, more input. It is the simple, radical act of sitting quietly in a room, and watching, and listening, and breathing.

I have been trying to do this, a little bit, every day. I sit in a chair by the window. I do not close my eyes or meditate in the formal sense. I just look. I see the neighbor’s cat climb the fence. I see the mailman walk his route. I see the clouds move, and the trees move in the wind, and the light change from yellow to gold to gray. Sometimes the minutes crawl. Sometimes they fly. But always, when I leave the chair, something has shifted. I am calmer. I am more connected. I remember that the world is real, that it exists independently of my worries, and that it is beautiful in a way that no screen can capture.

There is a poem by the British poet W.H. Auden called “Musée des Beaux Arts” about suffering and how it takes place “while someone else is eating or opening a window or just walking dully along.” He is talking about how the world ignores tragedy, but he is also, I think, pointing to the ordinariness of life as its greatest mystery. The miracles are not the spectacular ones; they are the everyday ones. The miracle of a child’s laugh. The miracle of a cup of hot tea on a cold morning. The miracle of a stranger’s smile. These are the things that sustain us, and we barely notice them. To pay attention is to see the miracle. To pay attention is to be alive.

In the end, that is what I want. Not to be successful or important or remembered, but to be alive, fully alive, to every moment that I am given. And I am learning that the way to be alive is to pay attention. To look. To listen. To taste. To touch. To be open, vulnerable, and willing to be affected by the world. The universe is indifferent, perhaps, but it is also astonishing. Every blade of grass is a testament to the improbability of existence. Every human face is a history of joy and sorrow. Every ordinary moment is a gift that will never come again. The least I can do is show up for it.

I sat on that bench outside the post office for a long time, watching the world go by. The pigeon finished its meal, the woman returned to her life, the cloud moved on. I did not have any great revelation. I did not solve any problem. But when I stood up to leave, I felt different. I had been somewhere. I had not been thinking about elsewhere. I had been here, and here had been enough.

That was a few years ago. I have not always lived up to the lesson of that afternoon. I have slipped back into the scrolling, the worrying, the chronic absent-mindedness. But the memory stays with me, a kind of beacon. And I know that I can return to that place whenever I choose, not the bench, but the state of mind. It is just a matter of attention. It is just a matter of deciding that what is right in front of me matters, and that I have the ability, and the privilege, to see it.

The writer Mary Oliver ended one of her poems with a question: “Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?” I used to think that the answer had to be something grand: achieve, create, change the world. Now I think it might be simpler. I think the answer might be to pay attention, to live in wonder, to accept the world’s gifts with open hands, and to give them back with open eyes. The world is full of noise, but it is also full of silence, and in the silence, if we can find it, we hear the true heartbeat of things. That heartbeat is not made by us. But we can listen to it. We can be moved by it. We can carry it within us, and let it shape the way we walk through the days of our lives.

So write freely, you asked. This is what I want to write: that attention is the beginning of love, that presence is the beginning of peace, and that the ordinary world is holy ground. The bread is on the table. The light is on the floor. The bird is at the window. And because we are here, because we are conscious, because we can see and hear and feel, we are already participants in an astonishing mystery. Do not let it go unnoticed.

I sat on that bench outside the post office for a long time, watching the world go by. The pigeon finished its meal, the woman returned to her life, the cloud moved on. I had been here, and here had been enough.

That was a few years ago. I have not always lived up to the lesson of that afternoon. I have slipped back into the scrolling, the worrying, the chronic absent-mindedness. But the memory stays with me, a kind of beacon. And I know that I can return to that place whenever I choose, not the bench, but the state of mind. It is just a matter of attention. It is just a matter of deciding that what is right in front of me matters, and that I have the ability, and the privilege, to see it.

The writer Mary Oliver ended one of her poems with a question: “Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?” I used to think that the answer had to be something grand: achieve, create, change the world. Now I think it might be simpler. I think the answer might be to pay attention, to live in wonder, to accept the world’s gifts with open hands, and to give them back with open eyes. The world is full of noise, but it is also full of silence, and in the silence, if we can find it, we hear the true heartbeat of things. That heartbeat is not made by us. But we can listen to it. We can be moved by it. We can carry it within us, and let it shape the way we walk through the days of our lives.

So write freely, you asked. This is what I want to write: that attention is the beginning of love, that presence is the beginning of peace, and that the ordinary world is holy ground. The bread is on the table. The light is on the floor. The bird is at the window. And because we are here, because we are conscious, because we can see and hear and feel, we are already participants in an astonishing mystery. Do not let it go unnoticed.
